resources.string: Affects only what the Network tool displays — no app feature depends on it. When on, the IP of each connection is looked up to show a host name (a reverse-DNS query); those lookups are the only network traffic this app itself sends. When off, connections just show the owner (e.g. Google) and the IP, and the app sends nothing.

Stream recordings to a machine on your network running the collector script — kept in SQLite with no on-device row limit. Great for long capture runs. When on, each monitor tool can choose to also stream to it while recording.

Run ./tools/collect.sh on your computer (starts the collector; sets up USB and asks which device if several are connected), then open http://localhost:8899 for guided setup, copy-paste URLs and live results. Enter the http://<your-ip>:<port> it shows here — or, over USB, use http://127.0.0.1:8899.
Couldn\'t reach the collector. Check the URL, that it\'s running, and that both devices are on the same network.

%1$d apps declare %2$d distinct permissions between them. By default only apps you can see and manage are shown — turn on system apps to include the platform\'s own.
Every permission carries one protection level, set by whoever defined it. This is the primary badge.
Guards private data or sensitive actions — location, camera, contacts. Asked for at runtime and can be revoked any time.
Special access granted from a Settings screen, not the runtime prompt — draw over other apps, install packages, all-files access.
Only granted to apps signed with the same key as the app that defined it. A normal app can request one but won\'t be granted it.
Low-risk; granted automatically at install with no prompt — internet, vibrate, set alarm.

Defined by an app rather than the Android platform. This is separate from protection level — a custom permission still has one, so it also counts under Dangerous, Signature, and so on. That\'s why the category totals add up to more than the permission count.

With Shizuku or root connected you can flip a permission on or off for an app right here — tap a permission (or a matrix cell) to open its sheet and use the switch. Dangerous permissions toggle with pm; special app-op permissions (all-files access, draw over apps, install unknown apps…) toggle with appops. Signature and normal permissions are fixed at install and stay read-only.
Connect Shizuku or root to grant or revoke permissions.

Runs in the background and stores every app-op access and denial as it happens — building history that outlasts the live snapshot. Keeps the newest rows up to the limit.

Every time an app touches a protected resource — location, camera, microphone, contacts and so on — Android records it as an app-op access. This is a device-wide log of those accesses, newest first, read live from the system.
The app was not on screen and had no visible service. A background camera, microphone or location hit is the thing most worth questioning.
The app was open and on screen when it made the access.
The app was running a foreground service (an ongoing notification), e.g. navigation or music.
A persistent system process. Expected for the platform itself.
The log is what the system currently holds — it trims over time and resets on reboot, so it shows recent activity rather than a complete history. Pull Refresh to re-read it.

Storage will read the system activity log through Shizuku and record every activity intent launched on the device — action, data, target and caller. It runs as a background service with a permanent notification and keeps going even if you close the app, until you press Stop.
When the limit is reached, the oldest events are deleted. Events are stored on-device in a database.

Android apps ship as portable bytecode. ART can compile it ahead-of-time to native machine code for faster startup and execution, at the cost of disk space. Pick how much to compile below — the current state and footprint update after each run.

This app is debuggable, so Android keeps it at “verify” and won\'t ahead-of-time compile it — these actions won\'t change the state or size. Try a normal (release) app to see them take effect.
Compile the hot methods from the usage profile. Balanced — what the system normally uses.
Compile every method to native. Fastest startup and runtime, larger on disk.
Compile all code, even rarely used. Maximum optimization, biggest footprint.
No native compilation — interpret + JIT. Smallest on disk; slower first runs.
Clear compiled artifacts back to the app\'s default state.
Hot methods compiled from the profile — balanced.
